world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Magaspag, Chie E. 2012. Language use and attitudes of Kachok speakers. MA thesis, Payap University (Payap server unreachable)

new_statements.quote: In a Kachok sesquisyllable, or prosodic word, the major syllable occurs word-finally and bears word-level stress. If present, the pre-syllable precedes the major syllable. Therefore, word stress in Kachok is always word-final and always falls on the major syllable, as discussed in Section 2.1. [p. 57] ... Pre-syllables are always unstressed. [p. 64]
new_statements.citation: Olsen, Emily L. 2018. The Sound Patterns of Kachok in the Context of Bahnaric and North-Bahnaric Studies. PhD dissertation, The Graduate Center, City University of New York.
new_statements.locator: Section 2.2.2 'Major Syllables: Stress', p. 57 (PDF p. 69); supporting statement sec. 2.3.2 'Pre-Syllables: Stress', p. 64 (PDF p. 76)
new_statements.rule_in_words: The prosodic word is a sesquisyllable: an optional reduced pre-syllable plus an obligatory heavy major syllable, and the major syllable is always word-final and carries the word stress. Stress is therefore fixed on the last syllable of the word; the pre-syllable never bears stress or any other suprasegmental feature (nasality, register/voice quality, length).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not treated as a word-level category. In compounds Olsen transcribes 'sesquisyllabic stress' with a secondary mark on the first element (e.g. ˌmiʔˈma̤ʔ 'parents', ˌmohˈmat 'face', p. 149), while fully transparent compounds keep two independent primary stresses (ˈçakˈmat 'eyelashes').
new_statements.exceptions: None for native words; Olsen states the maximal word is two syllables (pre-syllable + major syllable) and that disyllabic iambs and other shapes are under-represented and unstable. Loanwords from non-sesquisyllabic languages (Khmer, English) are adapted so that 'all of them presently have word-final stress and a heavy major syllable' (p. 152); trisyllabic or trochaic foreign names are repeated back as iambs with final stress (pp. 155-156). Phrase-level stress can fall on a function word that is promoted to a prosodic word by vowel lengthening (ex. 3, p. 137).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (the prosodic word = foot = sesquisyllable); based on elicited citation forms and recordings from Lower Kachut village, Andoung Meas district, collected in 2016-2017. Phrase-level stress is mentioned separately.
new_statements.identity_note: Olsen 2018 describes the Kachok of Kachut village (Upper/Lower Kachut, Andoung Meas district, Ratanakiri, Cambodia), i.e. ISO xkk = Glottolog kaco1239 itself, not the Romam variety of Vietnam (ISO rmx) which Glottolog treats separately. Olsen treats Romam as a closely related language and cites it only for comparison. The ISO 2021-018 change request added 'Kachok' as an alternate name for the same code, so 'Kaco'' and 'Kachok' are one language.

sources.locator: Section 2.2.2 'Major Syllables: Stress', p. 57 (PDF p. 69); supporting statement sec. 2.3.2 'Pre-Syllables: Stress', p. 64 (PDF p. 76)
sources.note: Sec. 2.2.2 'Major Syllables: Stress' (p. 57): word stress is always word-final and always falls on the major syllable of the sesquisyllable; sec. 2.3.2 (p. 64): pre-syllables are always unstressed. Compounds carry 'sesquisyllabic stress' with secondary stress on the first element (p. 149); phrase-level stress on a lengthened monosyllable noted in ex. (3) (p. 137); loanwords are adapted to word-final (iambic) stress (p. 152).
